children: By Jared Malsin and Chelsey Dulaney
ISTANBUL-Turkish authorities rushed to contain the fallout from the implosion of a series of investment funds that held billions of dollars, heaping fresh stress on Turkey's troubled economy.

Investors scrambled to cash out investments after a fund manager popular among everyday investors said it lacked the money to pay back clients. The rush triggered a selloff in the Istanbul stock market this week, spreading pain to dozens of similar funds.
Turkey's financial regulatory agency froze trading by seven asset managers and announced plans to liquidate 131 individual investment funds.

Everyday investors in Turkey have poured into stock trading as a way to protect themselves against years of high inflation. Asset managers and brokerages launched special funds that promised astronomical returns and few restrictions.

These funds often made big, risky bets on a small number of illiquid stocks and amplified gains by trading on margin-or with borrowed money. Some funds channeled investor money primarily into companies linked to them, according to investors and fund disclosures.

The flagship fund of one firm, Tera Portföy, reported returns of nearly 43,000% over the past two years. Before it was closed this week, the fund had attracted around 100,000 investors and had $5 billion in assets. The firm didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

"It was very obvious to everyone there was something wrong, but there was no regulatory action to stop this behavior," said Emre Akcakmak, a senior adviser at asset manager East Capital Group in Dubai.

The crisis poses an important challenge for the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his high-profile finance minister, Mehmet Simsek, an investor favorite who helped stabilize the Turkish economy after he returned to the post in 2023.
Simsek sought to reassure investors this week amid fears that hundreds of thousands of people including many ordinary Turkish citizens could lose money in the fund collapse.
"There's no systemic risk and as of now, markets are functioning as they should," Simsek said in an interview on Friday with Turkey's NTV, a national news channel.

Turkey has the largest economy of any Middle East nation and is also a member of the G-20 and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Erdogan's government has an outsize role as a military and diplomatic power broker in crises in both the Middle East and Europe.

Simsek positioned Istanbul as a potential global financial center and tried to persuade international companies and wealthy individuals to invest. Economists said the fund crisis illustrates the need for deeper reforms in Turkey's economic and judicial institutions.

Without reforms to improve oversight of the financial markets "you leave yourself vulnerable to this excess volatility and these market shocks," said Erik Meyersson, chief emerging-markets strategist at the Swedish bank SEB.
Turkey's government has responded to the fund crisis with a well-worn playbook of quickly casting blame and bringing in law enforcement.

Authorities detained and imposed travel bans on several executives linked to the investment companies, local media reported. Turkish authorities also referred 38 people to prosecutors for alleged financial crimes in connection with the scandal.
Last year, Simsek said the government was aware of manipulation in certain funds and pledged to crack down with stricter regulation.

In June, index provider MSCI said international investors had flagged "recurring instances of possible coordinated trading" by some Turkish funds and complained of other distortions in the market. MSCI warned it could review Turkey's emerging-market designation, which places it a rung higher than the world's least developed economies.
Foreign investors use MSCI's stock and bond indexes to guide their own portfolios and can be a crucial driver of investment.

"This [warning] was important from a prestige point of view as well as for attracting foreign investment. You don't want to be downgraded and go to the second division if you play in the first division," said Akcakmak of East Capital. "With that, the regulatory action likely accelerated."

Turkey's stock market is a relative minnow compared with larger, developed markets, with a total market capitalization of around $400 billion. After repeated currency crises and a long stretch of unorthodox monetary policy earlier this decade, foreign investors have pulled back from the market.

In late August, regulators imposed new limits on funds' investments in related parties and overall portfolio concentration. Investors began to pull money from some of the funds. The parent company of one fund manager, Pusula Portföy, agreed to sell itself to rival Tera Group as it struggled to repay investors. By Wednesday, some of Tera's funds could also no longer meet redemption requests.
The meltdown spilled over into the broader stock market, with the benchmark Borsa Istanbul 100 tumbling 5.5% on Wednesday and triggering a circuit breaker.

The stock market stabilized on Thursday after the central bank injected liquidity into the financial system, placed the troubled funds under the control of banks and announced plans to dissolve them. Stocks fell again Friday. A benchmark index dropped around 8.5% for the week, but remains up 17% this year.
Moves in government bond and currency markets were relatively muted, giving some comfort that the turmoil was confined to the stock market.
Investors warn the fiasco will hurt Turkey's credibility.

"They need to move pretty quickly to restore faith and confidence in this market," said Timothy Ash, a senior sovereign strategist at BlueBay Asset Management and a close watcher of the Turkish economy.
